rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir recites اقتده with kasra on dāl and a kasra-colored hāʾ without reaching yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر (اقتده) بكسر الدال وبشم الهاء الكسر من غير بلوغ ياء

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Mujāhid calls the reading erroneous because the hāʾ is an uninflected pause marker that clarifies the preceding vowel.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر بن مجاهد (¬5): (وهذا غلط لأن هذه الهاء هاء وقف لا تعرب

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī rejects the charge of error: the hāʾ can be a pronoun for an implicit verbal noun, indicated by the verb; the verse and a poem illustrate this use.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (ليس بغلط، ووجهها أن تجعل الهاء كناية عن المصدر لا التي تلحق (¬1) للوقف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The hāʾ cannot refer to the Qurʾān because the verb already takes that object through the lām; on this reading اقتده means الاقتداء, and its hāʾ would be silent at pause.
rows.anchor: فالهاء كناية عن المصدر، ودل يدرسه على الدرس، ولا يجوز أن يكون ضمير القرآن

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The verbal-noun analysis supplies الاقتداء from اقتد; the regular pause form would silence the pronoun hāʾ, as in اشتره.
rows.anchor: فكذلك قراءة ابن عامر: {فبهداهم اقتده} يكون اقتد الاقتداء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains that the Prophet asks them for no money in return.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: مالا تعطونيه)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says the Prophet seeks neither a fee for the Qurʾān nor a provision.
rows.anchor: وقال [الكلبي] (¬2): (جعلا على القرآن ولا رزقا)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the Qurʾān as a reminder and admonition for all creation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: موعظة للخلق أجمعين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān reminds people of what servants need for their religion through clear proof and eloquent admonition.
rows.anchor: فالقرآن هو المذكر بكل ما يحتاج إليه العباد في دينهم من حجة بينة وموعظة بليغة

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Following the prophets includes their practice of asking no payment to call people to God and explain truth to seekers; the command not to ask a wage makes that connection explicit.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (قوله تعالى: {قل لا أسألكم عليه أجرا} مما أمر به من هدى النبيين

rows.speaker: أهل العلم
rows.claim: They infer that Muḥammad’s law and earlier prophetic laws are one: what is established from a prophet remains binding unless abrogated.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل العلم: (وهذه الآية تدل على أن شريعة محمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وشريعة الأنبياء الماضين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command answers the polytheists’ taunt that believers eat what they slaughter but reject what God causes to die; the fāʾ links to an implied command to be guided.
rows.anchor: هذا جواب لقول المشركين: أتأكلون ما قتلتم ولا تأكلون ما قتل ربكم؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The food is that slaughtered while invoking God’s name; al-Zajjāj glosses it as slaughter sincerely dedicated to God.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (معناه: كلوا مما أخلصتم ذبحه لله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author maintains that pronouncing God’s name at slaughter is recommended Sunnah, not obligatory, referring to his discussion of 2:173.
rows.anchor: وقد ذكرنا عند قول تعالى (¬3): {وما أهل به لغير الله} [البقرة: 173] إن التسمية لا تجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional encourages belief in the permission to eat properly slaughtered food and confirms that what the law permits is wholesome; regarding it as impure opposes the verse, though personal aversion after accepting its permissibility is harmless.
rows.anchor: ترغيب في اعتقاد صحة الإذن في أكل المذكاة على اسم الله تعالى، وتأكيد أن ما أباحه الشرع فهو طيب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the forbidden food as carrion, including strangled, beaten, fallen, gored, and predator-eaten animals.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬5): (يريد: الميتة {والمنخنقة والموقوذة والمتردية

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī includes animals that die before slaughter can be completed and animals slaughtered for other than God.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (يعني: ما لم يذك ومات قبل أن تدرك ذكاته

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj glosses the prohibition as food whose slaughter was not made sincere for God.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (أي: مما لم يخلص ذبحه الله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it is grave disobedience” refers to the inferred act of eating; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses fisq as disobedience, while its lexical sense is departure from truth and religion.
rows.anchor: الهاء تعود على الأكل المدلول عليه، يعني: وإن الأكل لفسق

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes take the devils as Iblīs and his forces and their allies as polytheists and people of error, incited to dispute with Muḥammad and his Companions over carrion.
rows.anchor: وأكثر المفسرين: (على أن المراد بالشياطين هاهنا: إبليس وجنوده، وسوسوا إلى أوليائهم

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reports that rebellious Persian Magians wrote to their Qurashī allies after carrion was forbidden, taunting Muslims for accepting their slaughter but rejecting what God causes to die; some Muslims were unsettled and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة (¬7): ({وإن الشياطين} يعني: مردة المجوس {ليوحون إلى أوليائهم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obeying the polytheists by declaring carrion lawful would make the believers polytheists.
rows.anchor: ثم قال: {وإن أطعتموهم} يعني: في استحلال الميتة {إنكم لمشركون}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq generalizes that whoever permits what God forbids or forbids what He permits is a polytheist, since following another besides God associates that other with Him.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا دليل أن كل من أحل شيئا مما حرم الله، أو حرم شيئا مما أحل الله فهو مشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects applying the verse to a Muslim who omits the invocation: exegetes identify its subject as carrion and similar forbidden meat, not a Muslim’s slaughter without the formula.
rows.anchor: إن جميع المفسرين فسروا الآية بالميتة، وأشباهها، مما ذكره ابن عباس ولم يحملها أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three contextual clues establish that the subject is carrion: its eating is fisq, the dispute by consensus concerned carrion, and shirk here is permitting carrion rather than slaughter lacking invocation.
rows.anchor: ولا يفسق أكل ذبيحة المسلم الذي ترك التسمية بالإجماع

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses دينا as an accusative licensed by the sense: “guided me to a straight path” implies “made me know a religion.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أما نصب {دينا} فمحمول على المعنى

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Alternatively, دينا may be apposition to the meaning of “a straight path,” as in “guide you to a straight path.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون على البدل من معنى {إلى صراط مستقيم} لأن معناه: هداني صراطا مستقيما دينا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses قيما as straight; al-Akhfash and al-Zajjāj agree.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {قيما} قال ابن عباس: (يريد: مستقيما)

rows.speaker: أهل الكوفة
rows.claim: The Kufans read قيما with kasra on qāf and a light yāʾ; al-Zajjāj treats it as a verbal noun like الصغر and الكبر.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل (¬6) الكوفة {قيما} مكسورة القاف خفيفة الياء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says the expected form would retain wāw, as in العوض and الحول, but this form is anomalous like ثيرة and جياد.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: (وكان القياس أن يصحح فيه الواو كالعوض والحول

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses ملة as apposition to دينا قيما and حنيفا as an accusative circumstantial qualifier of Abraham. The sense is that God guided and taught the speaker Abraham’s religion in Abraham’s state of pure monotheism, the more apt attachment given the closing denial of his polytheism.
rows.anchor: وهو هاهنا لإبراهيم أحسن منه لغيره لقوله: {وما كان من المشركين}؛ قاله (¬5) أبو إسحاق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “you made me stray” as “you misled me,” comparing Noah’s statement in 11:34.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: فبما أضللتني، مثل قول نوح: {إن كان الله يريد أن يغويكم}

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī, citing linguists, says igwāʾ is causing misguidance to enter the heart and ghayy is blameworthy conduct; this caused Satan’s exit from the Garden.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر الأنباري حاكيا عن أهل اللغة: (الإغواء (¬4) إيقاع الغي في القلب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another linguistic view makes igwāʾ mean destruction, as in 19:59; this is linguistically possible, but exegetes prefer the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: قال: وقال بعضهم: الإغواء الإهلاك، ومنه قوله تعالى: {فسوف يلقون غيا} [مريم: 59]

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq reports two glosses of أغويتني: “you misled me,” or “you called me to something through which I went astray,” meaning because of Adam.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (في {أغويتني} قولان: قال بعضهم: أضللتني

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: One parse makes the bāʾ an oath, “by Your causing me to stray”; the lām answers the oath and Satan pledges to lie in wait on the straight path by God’s power, beautifying falsehood and sins.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: (وأما قوله عز وجل: {فبما}؛ فإن الباء تحتمل أمرين: أحدهما: القسم

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: In the oath parse, mā is a verbal noun and أغويتني its relative clause, with no resumptive pronoun.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان الباء قسما كان اللام جواب القسم، و (ما) بتأويل المصدر و {أغويتني} صلتها ولا عائد لها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Alternatively, mā is conditional and the bāʾ belongs to igwāʾ; the response’s fāʾ is omitted, as in the cited examples.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون (ما) بتأويل الشرط والباء من صلة الإغواء، والفاء المضمرة جواب الشرط

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj supplies an omitted على before the path; grammarians agree on the ellipsis, like saying someone struck a person on the back and stomach.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (أي: على طريقك المستقيم، ولا اختلاف بين النحويين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ explains this as “on their path and in it”: omission of the preposition is possible because a road functions semantically as a ظرف.
rows.anchor: وزاد الفراء بيانا، فقال (¬1): (المعنى -والله أعلم-: لأقعدن لهم على طريقهم وفي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the straight path as God’s clear religion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في تفسير {صراطك المستقيم} (يريد: دينك الواضح)

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd identifies the straight path as God’s Book.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود: (هو كتاب الله)

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh identifies the straight path as Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال جابر بن عبد الله: (هو الإسلام)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In ʿAṭāʾ’s narration from Ibn ʿAbbās, when people of the Heights enter Paradise, people of Hell hope for relief and ask God to let them see their relatives there. Paradise is adorned; the groups see one another, but people of Paradise do not recognize their changed relatives. The people of Hell call them by name and ask for water.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (لما صار أصحاب الأعراف إلى الجنة طمع أهل النار بفرج بعد الإياس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and al-Suddī explain “what God provided you” as food.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد والسدي: (يعني: الطعام)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq says human beings need food and drink even while being punished; people of Paradise tell them God has forbidden their food and drink to people of Hell.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: (أعلم الله عز وجل أن ابن آدم غير مستغن عن الطعام والشراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition is one of deprivation, not a ritual or devotional prohibition.
rows.anchor: [و] هذا (¬6) تحريم منع لا تحريم تعبد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses those who made their religion amusement and play as mockers and al-muqtasimīn.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس (¬1): (يريد: المستهزئين المقتسمين)

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: They define lahw as diverting concern with something useless; these people distracted themselves by mocking religion and criticizing believers. “Their religion” means the religion prescribed for them, which they treated as a game.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني (¬3) (معنى اللهو: صرف الهم بما لا يحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says God leaves them in Hell as they left belief in this Day; their forgetting means denying resurrection, Paradise, and Hell.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: نتركهم في جهنم كما تركوا لقاء يومهم هذا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says God leaves them in punishment as they left work for the meeting with the Day; al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Suddī, and all exegetes likewise take forgetting to mean leaving.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (أي: نتركهم في عذابهم كما تركوا العمل للقاء يومهم)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī stresses that God does not leave them through inadvertence: they are deliberately left in the Fire as they deliberately abandoned deeds for that Day.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: (فاليوم نتركهم في النار على غير إغفال ونسيان

rows.speaker: أصحاب المعاني
rows.claim: God treats them like the forgetful by leaving them in Hell, requiting their turning from revelations and commands with matching abandonment: their prayers go unanswered and their pleas receive no mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال أصحاب المعاني: (معنى {ننساهم كما نسوا}: نعاملهم معاملة من نسي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the phrase means “as they denied”; ما is genitive by coordination with كما, and both occurrences of ما are verbal nouns, giving the sense “as they left this Day and for their denial of Our signs.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (أي: كجحدهم (¬2)، {وما} في موضع جر نسق على {كما}

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī gives the resulting construction: God leaves them with a forgetting like their forgetting this Day, and because they denied the signs.
rows.anchor: والتقدير: ننساهم نسيانا كنسيانهم يومهم هذا ولكونهم جاحدين بآياتنا، قاله أبو علي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the Book brought to them as the one Muḥammad brought and glosses “We detailed it” as “We clarified it.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: الذي جاء به محمد - صلى الله عليه وسلم -، {فصلناه} يريد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafsīl means clarifying meanings by distinguishing them from what could be confused; it is equivalent to tabyīn.
rows.anchor: والتفصيل تبيين المعاني بإظهارها مما يلتبس بها، فالتفصيل كالتبيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With knowledge” means God detailed the Book without oversight or mistake; another view takes it as the knowledge deposited in the Book, including sciences and rulings.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {على علم} أي: فصلناه بعلم لم يقع منا فيه سهو ولا غلط

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj parses هدى as accusative, meaning “We detailed it as guidance and mercy.”
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: ({هدى} في موضع نصب أي: فصلناه هاديا وذا رحمة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb أنشر الله الريح means that God revived the wind and it came alive.
rows.anchor: يقال (¬3) أنشر الله الريح مثل أحياها فنشرت هي أي: حييت

rows.speaker: المرار
rows.claim: Al-Marrār’s verse uses أحييت of the breeze as evidence that wind can be described as living or reviving.
rows.anchor: قال المرار (¬5): وهبت له ريح الجنوب وأحييت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wind is also described as dying, so a second poem supports the language of wind’s life and death.
rows.anchor: ومما يدل على ذلك أن الريح قد وصفت بالموت كما وصفت بالحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: نشرا is plural of نشور, “spread out”; plural الرياح takes a plural adjective, while the singular reading الريح can mean many winds, as in collective singulars and الإنسان followed by plural believers.
rows.anchor: فقوله: {نشرا} جمع: نشور مثل رسول ورسل، والنشور بمعنى: المنتشر

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿĀmir reads نشرا with a light shīn, as in كتب and رسل.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر: {نشرا} خفف الشين كما يقال: كتب ورسل

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read نشرا as the verbal noun نشر, opposite of folding; the winds are spread after being folded, or the noun denotes life, or it is an absolute accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي {نشرا}؛ والنشر مصدر نشرت الشيء ضد طويته

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads بشرا as the plural of بشير, matching “winds bearing good news” in 30:46: they announce rain and mercy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم {بشرا} جمع بشيرا على (بشر)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says النشر describes the pleasant, gentle winds that form clouds.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (النشر من الرياح الطيبة اللينة التي تنشئ السحاب)

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī gives نشور as the singular and connects نشر to pleasant fragrance; the author cites an Imruʾ al-Qays poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: (واحدها نشور، وأصل هذا من النشر

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda glosses نشرا as winds dispersed from every direction.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: ({نشرا} أي: متفرقة من كل جانب)

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr glosses the winds as spread out and broad in their blowing; نشر means dispersal, as in spreading cloth or sawing wood.
rows.anchor: قال أبو بكر: (هي المنتشرة الواسعة الهبوب، والنشر: التفريق

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: The reading of Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī can be parsed by ellipsis as ذوات نشر, meaning fragrant winds.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: {نشرا} يجوز أن يكون من باب حذف المضاف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says “before His mercy” means before the rain.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: بين يدي المطر)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī glosses it as ahead of His rain.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (قدام مطره)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq takes the phrase as before the rain, which is God’s mercy.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق: (أي: بين يدي المطر الذي هو رحمته)

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr explains “the hands of” metaphorically as precedence: Arabs say trials are before the Hour, and winds precede and signal rain.
rows.anchor: اليدان تستعملهما العرب في المجاز على معنى التقدمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aqalla means to carry, as does istaqalla; the winds carry clouds heavy with water, according to the exegetes.
rows.anchor: يقال: أقل فلان الشيء أي (¬5) حمله، وكذلك استقله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sahāb is grammatically masculine although it is a collective form of sahāba, like tamr/tamra and jawz/jawza; this explains the masculine pronoun.
rows.anchor: والسحاب لفظه مذكر وإن كان جمع سحابة، لذلك ذكر الكناية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says a dead land is one without vegetation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: ليس فيه نبات)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbī says it is a place where nothing grows.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (إلى مكان لا ينبت)

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr explains the cloud is driven to a place needing rain because rain has ceased there; the lām can mean “toward” or “for the sake of.”
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر: (أي: سقنا السحاب لبلد وإلى بلد محتاج إلى المطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A balad is any part of earth, settled or unsettled, empty or inhabited; its subdivision is a baldah, plural bilād, and wilderness can also be called baldah. Al-Aʿshā’s line uses بلد for a desolate wilderness.
rows.anchor: وأما البلد فكل موضع من الأرض عامر أو غير عامر خال أو مسكون فهو بلد

rows.speaker: الزجاج وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj and Ibn al-Anbārī say “We sent down water by it” can mean by the land or by the cloud, since cloud is the instrument for sending down water.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج وابن الأنباري (¬2): (جائز أن يكون فأنزلنا بالبلد الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent referent of the pronoun in “by it We brought forth” is water, because fruit is brought out by water.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أن الكناية تعود إلى الماء؛ لأن إخراج الثمرات كان بالماء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj also permits taking the pronoun as the land, since the passage does not specify one particular land.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (وجائز أن يكون فأخرجنا بالبلد من كل الثمرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection of the dead is likened to bringing forth plants from the dead land.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {كذلك نخرج الموتى} أي: مثل ذلك الإخراج الذي أشرنا إليه

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abū Bakr makes the analogy explicit: reviving the dead after they have become remains in the soil is like reviving earth with vegetation.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر: (أي: نحيي الموتى مثل ذلك الإحياء الذي وصفناه في البلد الميت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “so that you may remember” as “so that you may take admonition.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: كي تتعظوا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says the evidence should lead people to infer God’s oneness and resurrection; laʿalla expresses hope from the human addressees’ perspective, since God knows whether they will heed it and people speak according to what they know and hope from others.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: (أي: لعلكم بما بينا (¬2) لكم تستدلون على توحيد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chiefs’ words incite Pharaoh against Moses and protest allowing him to remain in opposition.
rows.anchor: هذا إغراء من الملأ وتحريض لفرعون على موسى، وإنكار أن يتركه مقيما على مخالفته

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr reports that Pharaoh was terrified of Moses and would urinate like a donkey when he saw him; the chiefs did not know of this fear and thought he was violating royal custom by failing to crush opposition, unaware he could not overcome Moses.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير: (كان فرعون قد ملئ رعبا من موسى، وكان إذا رآه بال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains the alleged corruption as worshipping God and affirming His oneness.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: يعبدوا الله ويوحدوه)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes corruption as calling people to reject Pharaoh’s worship and exposing his ignorance; the author says this amounts to Ibn ʿAbbās’s explanation.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: (أراد بالإفساد في الأرض دعاؤهم الناس إلى مخالفة فرعون

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī parses ويذرك as shifted coordination from the first verb: would Pharaoh let Moses corrupt the land when he has left off obeying Pharaoh and worshipping his gods? Al-Farrāʾ agrees, citing Ubayy’s variant.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري: (إنه ينتصب على الصرف (¬6) عن الأول

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading “they have left off worshipping you” supports that parse.
rows.anchor: واحتج على هذا بقراءة أبي: (أتذر موسى وقومه ليفسدوا في الأرض وقد تركوا

rows.speaker: بعض النحويين
rows.claim: Some grammarians treat the wāw as replacing fāʾ, giving “then he will leave you and your gods”; Abū Isḥāq adopts this analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض النحويين: الواو نائبة عن الفاء، والتقدير: فيذرك وآلهتك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abū Isḥāq parses ويذرك as the response to the question with a wāw: would Pharaoh let Moses, and then Moses would leave him?
rows.anchor: وهذا قول أبي إسحاق، قال: (نصب {ويذرك} على جواب الاستفهام بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds it far-fetched to parse ويذرك like يفسدوا: the singular addressee and plural يفسدوا show it is detached from that verb.
rows.anchor: وحمله بعض الناس على إعراب (يفسدوا)، وفي هذا بعد؛ لأن توحيده مع جمع (يفسدوا)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās rejects the common reading وآلهتك and reads وإلاهتك, “your worship”; on that reading Pharaoh worshipped and was not worshipped. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Masʿūd, al-Shaʿbī, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq also read it so.
rows.anchor: كان ابن عباس ينكر قراءة العامة ويقرأ: (وإلاهتك) أي: عبادتك

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains وإلاهتك as “your lordship,” equivalent to ربوبتك.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: (والمعنى: ويذرك وربوبيتك ف (إلاهتك) بمنزلة ربوبيتك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading وآلهتك is the plural of إله, on the pattern إزار وآزرة.
rows.anchor: وقرأ العامة {وآلهتك} على جمع إله مثل إزار وآزرة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Pharaoh made small idols for his people to worship while claiming to be their lord and theirs, explaining “I am your highest lord”; al-Zajjāj gives a similar account.
rows.anchor: فقد روي عن ابن عباس أنه قال: (كان فرعون صنع لقومه أصناما صغارا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says Pharaoh himself worshipped idols, so he both worshipped and was worshipped.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: (كان فرعون يعبد الأصنام)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says Pharaoh worshipped whichever cow he found beautiful and ordered his people to worship it; this is linked to the Samaritan calf, and a similar account is from Sulaymān al-Taymī.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (كان يعبد ما يستحسن من البقر، وكانوا إذا رأوا بقرة حسناء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Pharaoh had stopped killing Israelite sons, but after Moses came with the message Pharaoh ordered the killings resumed.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (كان فرعون قد ترك قتل أبناء بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The chiefs urged Pharaoh to kill Moses, but he did not dare because of Moses’ power and standing; instead he weakened the Israelites by killing their sons and keeping their daughters alive for labor and service.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: (إنما دعي فرعون إلى قتل موسى، لكنه لم يطمع في ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses “we are dominant over them” as “we are able to do so.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: وإنا على ذلك قادرون)
